svg.title: Four ways to record complete-arch implant positions
svg.desc: Conventional splinted open-tray impression with a verified stone cast, the long-standing reference. Intraoral scanning with scan bodies, splinted or non-splinted, which is technique-sensitive across an edentulous arch because the mucosa offers few landmarks for stitching. Photogrammetry, intraoral or extraoral, which in systematic reviews showed better trueness and precision than intraoral scanning but captures only implant positions, so a tissue and bite scan is still needed. Reverse scan, where the interim prosthesis or a verification jig with scan analogs is scanned outside the mouth, which is only as good as that prosthesis or jig fits. A footer reminds that whatever method you use, verify before you make the definitive prosthesis.

g.text: Recording implant positions — four routes
1 · Splinted open-tray (analog)
Reference standard · verified stone cast
Slower; material, splint and pour errors
Still the benchmark in comparison studies
2 · Intraoral scan + scan bodies
stitching path
Fast, in-office; ~88 µm vs conventional (36 jaws)
Featureless mucosa → stitching error grows
across the arch; splinting/aids help variably
3 · Photogrammetry (PG)
Coded targets read by cameras; very fast
Better trueness/precision than IOS in reviews
Positions only → still scan tissue + bite
Cost; system-specific libraries
4 · Reverse scan (extraoral)
Scan the provisional or a jig on scan analogs
Copies an approved design to the final
Only valid if that prosthesis/jig fits passively
Any route → verify (jig / rigid prototype try-in + radiographs) before the definitive prosthesis
